Oh I agree. I was trying to make a different point.

The idea that it's good to examine your own beliefs, either to strengthen then with a deeper understanding, or to open the door to modify them and thus grow, seems so sensible as to be beyond question. But it's hardly a universally accepted idea. It's quite uncommon in about half the world right now, and it was considered kind of revolutionary and subversive just a few hundred years ago, even here in the west.

You hold this belief, I'll guess, along with several others; a basically secular world view, a confidence in the value of science and knowledge, a sense that things get better as the world around us is better understood and more confidently manipulated. Freely expressing and debating ideas is a key part of this too, as is a general sense of your own sovereignty, which means that no other person is more than your equal. This package of ideas used to be called liberalism, and now it's called 'classical liberalism', and it was a fresh hot topic right around the time of the American revolution.

People in China generally don't think this way. People in Muslims lands are often overtly hostile to it. Indigenous people might have trouble even conceptualizing it.

It's not a given, not an objective thing. Your allegiance to these ideas is based on belief, on faith.

Don't get me wrong, I'm not minimizing this in the least. I'll take it a step further and say that everyone's allegiance to everything is based on faith, if you dig down to the roots of it. This is not a problem, it's just how our minds work. Our values and our alignments are necessarily subjective things.

You can look at love the same way. Love is arguably the most important thing, and yet it's honestly just a subjective feeling. It can be the strongest thing in the world and it can shatter with a single word. It's everything and nothing. All of it, everything we believe, everything we align ourselves with, everything that becomes our identities, is rooted in stubborn gut feeling and nothing else.

That's not a bad thing, or even an avoidable thing, it's just how it is.

If you agree (and of course you might not) and if you can shrug and say, yeah, I guess I'm like that, then it's a lot easier to understand the stubbornness you see in others. They might still be wrong, and they might still be a pain in the ass, but you can understand them, and that's a pretty cool thing just by itself.
